content: When a cesarean delivery is performed before the onset of labor in a woman with intact amniotic membranes, the risk of early-onset Group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease among full-term infants is extremely low. However, data on the risk of transmission to preterm infants born via cesarean delivery under similar conditions are limited. Nevertheless, the risk of transmission in such cases is likely much lower than in vaginal deliveries or cesarean deliveries performed after membrane rupture or labor onset. The timing of specimen collection for GBS screening is critical because GBS colonization status can change during pregnancy. Colonization early in pregnancy is not predictive of early-onset GBS disease, as colonization can be transient. Late third-trimester colonization status is often used as a proxy for intrapartum colonization. GBS cultures performed within five weeks of delivery have a negative predictive value of 95%-98%. However, the clinical utility of prenatal cultures decreases when performed more than five weeks before delivery, as the negative predictive value declines. Swabbing both the lower vagina and rectum (through the anal sphincter) significantly increases the culture yield compared to sampling the cervix or vagina alone. While some studies have evaluated the ability of perianal or vaginal-perianal cultures to detect GBS colonization, data comparing their performance to vaginal-rectal cultures are limited. Studies have shown that when women in outpatient clinic settings collect their own vaginal-rectal screening specimens with proper instruction, the GBS yield is comparable to specimens collected by healthcare providers. The use of appropriate transport media can maintain the viability of GBS in settings where immediate laboratory processing is not possible. GBS isolates can remain viable in transport media for several days at room temperature, but recovery declines over 1-4 days, especially at high temperatures. Sensitivity is highest when specimens are stored at 4°C and processed within 24 hours of collection. Regardless of the test used to identify GBS, the use of an enrichment broth significantly improves detection. Direct agar plating without selective enrichment broth can result in up to 50% of GBS carriers having false-negative culture results. Examples of selective enrichment broths include Todd-Hewitt broth supplemented with either gentamicin and nalidixic acid or colistin and nalidixic acid. The addition of 5% sheep blood to broths like TransVag and Lim broth can further enhance GBS recovery. Some selective enrichment broths contain chromogenic substrates that change color in the presence of beta-hemolytic GBS, facilitating identification. However, non-hemolytic isolates will not be detected by these broths alone. Among 265 GBS isolates from invasive early-onset cases in the ABCs system areas during 2006-2008, 4% were non-hemolytic. Following enrichment, GBS is conventionally identified through subculture on blood agar plates and presumptive identification using the CAMP test or serologic identification with latex agglutination and group B streptococcal antisera. Chromogenic agars that change color in the presence of beta-hemolytic GBS colonies have also become available. These agars, like pigmented enrichment broths, facilitate the detection of beta-hemolytic GBS but do not detect non-hemolytic strains. Rapid techniques for identifying GBS directly from enrichment broth or after subculture have been developed, including DNA probes and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR). NAATs have shown high sensitivity and specificity compared to the gold standard of enrichment followed by subculture. Studies comparing intrapartum NAAT on non-enriched samples and late antepartum enriched culture results to intrapartum enriched culture have demonstrated varying sensitivities and specificities, with enrichment steps before testing improving detection rates.
